claims.statement: Every BFF Keycloak Admin REST API call authenticates by minting an admin token from a dedicated service account: getAdminToken() in keycloak.ts POSTs grant_type=client_credentials with keycloakServiceClientId/keycloakServiceClientSecret to the realm's token endpoint and returns the access_token, and any non-OK token response is mapped to an AuthError with code KEYCLOAK_UNAVAILABLE and HTTP status 503 (never 401), so a wrong or missing service-account secret is indistinguishable from Keycloak being down.

The service-account credentials are a separate client from the user-facing login client: env.ts defines keycloakServiceClientId (KEYCLOAK_SERVICE_CLIENT_ID, default mcm-bff-service) and keycloakServiceClientSecret alongside the distinct keycloakClientId (KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID) and keycloakClientSecret used for the authorization-code and refresh grants, so one client's credentials must not be reused for the other's grant type.

email-service.ts carries its own duplicated getAdminToken() rather than importing keycloak.ts's, to avoid a circular dependency, and the two copies are not identical: keycloak.ts's copy goes through a keycloakFetch wrapper that adds the request's X-Request-Id header while email-service.ts's copy calls bare fetch, and sendVerificationEmail reads the client id from env.keycloakClientId in one copy and keycloakConfig.clientId in the other — so a change to the grant parameters, error handling or endpoint has to be applied in both places.

A service account whose realm-management client roles are missing still authenticates, so the 503 token path never triggers, and Keycloak rejects each Admin API call with 403 which the BFF re-maps per caller instead of passing through: deleteUser, countUsersInClientRole, sendVerificationEmail and every step of assignMcUserRole answer 502 KEYCLOAK_UNAVAILABLE, createUser answers 400 INVALID_INPUT, ensureClientRedirectUris warns and retries, and logoutUserSessions ignores the failure entirely — a 403 is therefore never visible in a BFF response. The same per-function re-mapping applies to the 401 a token lacking the kc-admin-api client scope receives, so neither status is ever propagated.

deleteUser treats a 404 from the Admin API as success and throws KEYCLOAK_UNAVAILABLE with status 502 for any other non-OK response, because account deletion's identity step is the last and irreversible one and a retry after a partial failure re-issues the delete against an account the first attempt already removed — treating 404 as an error would make the retry fail exactly where it had otherwise worked.

ensureClientRedirectUris(uris, keycloakClientId) is a second Admin API path: it mints an admin token, looks the named client up by clientId, fetches the client's full representation, and PUTs it back with redirectUris [...existing, ...missing]. Feature 083 added the keycloakClientId parameter (defaulting to the login client) so the backup-consent client's own callback can be registered on that client, because on the login client alone Keycloak refuses the consent authorization request. Its entire body sits inside a try and no path rethrows — a service account without manage-clients or a Keycloak outage leaves the redirect URI unregistered while GET /bff-api/auth/init still answers {ok: true} — so every non-success path instead calls a local unrecorded(step, status) helper.

ensureClientRedirectUris is one-shot per Keycloak client id per process lifetime, tracked in a module-level Set, and the client id is recorded only when Keycloak confirmed the work — nothing was missing, or the PUT answered 2xx (feature 085, item #753). A rejected update, a failed client lookup or fetch, or a thrown error leaves the id absent from the Set, so the next GET /bff-api/auth/init retries the registration instead of skipping it permanently; before 085 a rejected PUT still latched the mark and an address that was never registered stayed that way until a restart.

The admin token is minted per call and never cached: each Admin API function in keycloak.ts calls getAdminToken() itself (unlike the OIDC discovery document, which is cached at module level), so one user-facing operation makes several token requests — registration mints for createUser, assignMcUserRole and sendVerificationEmail, and the resend-verification route mints once for getUserIdByEmail and again for sendVerificationEmail — and a rotated or mistyped service-account secret takes every Admin API call down at once rather than degrading it.

getUserIdByEmail returns null for any non-OK Admin response — indistinguishable from 'no such user' — and /bff-api/auth/resend-verification deliberately answers success for an unknown email so the endpoint is not a user-enumeration oracle, so a service account that lost view-users produces a success response while nothing was sent. Registration no longer shares that shape: since feature 092 assignMcUserRole status-checks all three of its calls and throws 502 KEYCLOAK_UNAVAILABLE on a refusal, so a registration cannot answer 201 with the mc-user role unassigned; what it leaves behind is the account createUser already created, because removing it is explicitly out of scope and a retry therefore meets the duplicate path instead.

The swallowed Admin API failures are not uniform and the differences are deliberate: deleteUser counts 404 as success for retry safety; logoutUserSessions and revokeToken ignore failures because the BFF session and token are already gone and the token expires naturally; and backup-offline-token.ts deliberately does not reuse revokeToken, reporting whether the revocation succeeded instead, because an offline refresh token never expires and so has no such backstop.

The account-deletion pipeline uses both credential sets in one ordered run: account-deletion.ts calls deleteUser and logoutUserSessions (service-account Admin API) alongside revokeToken (the app client's revoke endpoint), with deleteIdentity last because it is the only irreversible step — so a 503 from the Admin API steps says nothing about the token-revocation step, and deleteUser's 404-as-success rule is what makes a retry of that pipeline completable.

countUsersInClientRole throws KEYCLOAK_UNAVAILABLE with status 502 when the client lookup or the role-members listing fails, rather than returning 0, because a failed count must not read as 'no administrators exist' and let the last administrator delete themselves.

A Keycloak realm partial-export does not carry service-account role mappings, so the committed realm files reconstruct them explicitly as service-account-<clientId> users with realmRoles and clientRoles; without that reconstruction a partial import yields a service account that mints tokens and authorizes nothing, and every Admin API call it makes comes back 403.

The keycloakAdminApiBase used by every Admin API path is derived in env.ts from the internal keycloakUrl (runtime), not from the build-inlined browser-facing keycloakConfig, so Admin API calls reach Keycloak from inside a container over the internal service address.

Every non-success path of ensureClientRedirectUris reports itself through logger.warn('redirect_uri_registration_failed', { action: 'ensure_redirect_uris', step, status }), where step is one of client_lookup, client_fetch, update or error, and the payload deliberately carries no admin token, no client representation and no URI value; unit-tests/redirect-uri-registration.test.ts pins the event name, the step/status pairs, the absence of those values, and the per-client retry behaviour, using a distinct client id per case because the done mark is per client per process.

GET /bff-api/auth/init hands ensureClientRedirectUris the complete six-URI list for the login client (web PKCE callback, verified-email redirect, native login scheme URI, backup-consent callback, account-deletion step-up callback and its native scheme URI), and makes a second call for env.backupConsentClientId with only the backup-consent callback when that client differs from the login client; the live integration test asserts the consent callback is registered without dropping the pre-existing URIs and that a repeat call adds no duplicate.

The committed realm files separate the two clients by capability, not only by name: `mcm-bff-service` is a confidential client with `serviceAccountsEnabled: true`, `standardFlowEnabled: false` and a client-secret authenticator, while the login client `movie-collection-manager` has `standardFlowEnabled: true` and `serviceAccountsEnabled: false` — so the service-account client cannot run the authorization-code flow and the login client cannot mint a client-credentials token.

The service-account secret is shared across more than the BFF: the realm files declare `mcm-bff-service`'s secret as the placeholder `${KEYCLOAK_SERVICE_CLIENT_SECRET}`, which Keycloak resolves from the keycloak container env at `--import-realm`, and `scripts/gen-dev-env.mjs` projects the same value from `stacks/auth.env` into the BFF env files while first proving it with a real `client_credentials` grant against the running realm — it refuses to write (exit 2) when the realm rejects the credentials, because a realm and its env file drifting apart breaks realm-secret == BFF-secret everywhere. The same credentials are also read by `add-container-redirect-uris.mjs` (env var, falling back to `frontend/mcm-app/.env.docker`) and by `backup-consent-redirect-uri.integration.test.ts`, which skips itself unless `KEYCLOAK_SERVICE_CLIENT_SECRET` is set and throws when `MCM_REQUIRE_LIVE_STACK=1`.

A missing service-account secret is not a startup failure: `keycloakServiceClientSecret` is loaded with an empty-string fallback (`requireEnv('KEYCLOAK_SERVICE_CLIENT_SECRET', '')`), as is `keycloakClientSecret`, so an unset variable produces an empty `client_secret` on the token request instead of aborting boot — the failure appears only when an Admin-API-backed route is exercised, as the 503 KEYCLOAK_UNAVAILABLE from `getAdminToken()`.

assignMcUserRole status-checks each of its three Admin API calls — the client lookup, the mc-user role read and the role-mapping POST — and throws KEYCLOAK_UNAVAILABLE with status 502 on any refusal (feature 092, FR-004), so a refused role read stops the chain instead of posting the error body as if it were the role; unit-tests/keycloak-assign-role.test.ts pins a refused client lookup, a refused role read and a refused assignment as 502, asserts a successful run posts exactly the role representation, and its own header comment records the defect it replaces: production's client lookup was refused with 403 and the role-assignment POST was never checked at all, so a refusal there would have reported success for an account with no access — the 'No trace' half of the production defect, alongside a register route that logged nothing on failure.

POST /bff-api/auth/register logs logger.error('registration failed', { action: 'register_failed', ip, code, error }) only for statuses 500 and above and never includes the request body — no password, no email — while a refusal the caller caused (a duplicate username or email, a weak password, the disabled self-registration gate, a rate limit) is not logged as a server-side failure (feature 092, FR-005). tests/app/bff-api/auth/register+api.test.ts pins both the server-side log for a 502 without the body and its absence for a caller-caused 409.

From Keycloak 26.8.2 an Admin API token must carry the kc-admin-api client scope, and without it every BFF admin call is refused 401 with Expected audience not available in the token, because the 26.8.2 migration creates the scope and gives it only to admin-cli and security-admin-console. All three realm files must define the scope — including its oidc-admin-api-audience-mapper protocol mapper — as well as assign it to mcm-bff-service as a default client scope, because import ignores a reference to a scope the file does not define and logs Referenced client scope 'kc-admin-api' doesn't exist. Ignoring; an existing realm (production, or a local stack with an existing Postgres volume, since import is IGNORE_EXISTING) instead needs scripts/ensure-admin-api-scope.mjs, which reports what is missing and changes nothing without --apply, or the console route where the admin has two-factor and the script's password-only sign-in cannot be used.

The mcm-bff-service service-account roles differ deliberately by realm variant: prod-realm.json defines service-account-mcm-bff-service with exactly view-users, view-clients and manage-users, while ci-realm.json and dev-realm.json also carry manage-clients. manage-clients is withheld in production because it would let the BFF edit any client, and production needs no client write because movie-collection-manager already lists every address /bff-api/auth/init registers. query-clients is not a substitute for view-clients — the lookup answers 200 with an empty list, which the BFF reads as 'client not found'. scripts/__tests__/keycloak-service-account-roles.guard.test.mjs asserts the shared requirement, production's exact three roles, and that production lists every registered address.

Production's realm was configured by hand and drifted from what the BFF needs: prod-realm.json defined no service account at all, and production held manage-users, view-users, query-groups and query-users, so its client lookup answered 403 — account deletion failed for an administrator and registration created an account and then failed to give it a role. CI could not see any of it, because CI imports its own realm file into a fresh volume every run. Feature 092 recorded the requirement in prod-realm.json and added the realm guard, while the running realm is corrected by hand, since a realm file applies only when a realm is first created.

The register route's server-side failure log has one gap: it fires only for statuses 500 and above, and a service-account refusal on createUser is re-mapped to INVALID_INPUT with status 400, so that failure is answered to the caller as 'The provided information is invalid. Please check your input.' and is logged nowhere — unlike a refused role assignment, which surfaces as a 502 and is logged as register_failed.
